:question/problem "Consider the following initial value problem:

$$
{y}^{′}={x}^{2}-y,\,y(1)=1
$$

Using the trapezoidal method with step size $Δx=1,$ the new value ${y}_{\text{new}}$ is obtained by solving the equation $g({y}_{\text{new}})=0$ at each step. Which of the following is the **specific function** $g({y}_{\text{new}})$ used in the first step?" :question/worked-solution "For an initial value problem

$$
{y}^{′}=f(x,y),\,y(a)=c,
$$

the trapezoidal method with step size $Δx$ is given by

$$
Δy=\frac{1}{2}({y}^{′}+{y}_{\text{new}}^{′})\cdot Δx,
$$

with ${y}_{\text{new}}^{′}=f({x}_{\text{new}},{y}_{\text{new}})$ evaluated at the next $x$ and $y$ values.

In this example  $Δy$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}Δy & =\frac{1}{2}({y}^{′}+{y}_{\text{new}}^{′})\cdot Δx \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(({x}^{2}-y)+({x}_{\text{new}}^{2}-{y}_{\text{new}}))\cdot 1 \\  & =\frac{1}{2}({x}^{2}-y+{x}_{\text{new}}^{2}-{y}_{\text{new}}).\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting this into ${y}_{\text{new}}=y+Δy,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{\text{new}} & =y+Δy \\ {y}_{\text{new}} & =y+\frac{1}{2}({x}^{2}-y+{x}_{\text{new}}^{2}-{y}_{\text{new}}),\end{aligned}
$$

and moving all terms to the left-hand side gives the equation

$$
{y}_{\text{new}}-y-\frac{1}{2}({x}^{2}-y+{x}_{\text{new}}^{2}-{y}_{\text{new}})=0.
$$

So, the general form of the function $g$ for step size $Δx=1$ is

$$
g({y}_{\text{new}})={y}_{\text{new}}-y-\frac{1}{2}({x}^{2}-y+{x}_{\text{new}}^{2}-{y}_{\text{new}}).
$$

Now, in the first step, the new $x$ value is

$$
{x}_{\text{new}}=x+Δx=1+1=2.
$$

Therefore, the function used in the first step is

$$
\begin{aligned}g({y}_{\text{new}}) & ={y}_{\text{new}}-1-\frac{1}{2}({1}^{2}-1+{2}^{2}-{y}_{\text{new}}) \\  & ={y}_{\text{new}}-1-\frac{1}{2}(0+4-{y}_{\text{new}}) \\  & =\frac{3}{2}{y}_{\text{new}}-3.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186308572 :question/id #uuid "5954fe07-ca71-56cd-b722-9e93582b85a7" :question/math-academy-id "q-334151"} {:db/id 17592186377165 :question/id #uuid $$
{y}^{′}=f(x,y),\,y(a)=c,
$$

the trapezoidal method with step size $Δx$ is given by

$$
Δy=\frac{1}{2}({y}^{′}+{y}_{\text{new}}^{′})\cdot Δx,
$$

with ${y}_{\text{new}}^{′}=f({x}_{\text{new}},{y}_{\text{new}})$ evaluated at the next $x$ and $y$ values.

In this example, $Δy$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}Δy & =\frac{1}{2}({y}^{′}+{y}_{\text{new}}^{′})\cdot Δx \\  & =\frac{1}{2}({x}^{2}\sqrt{y}+({x}_{\text{new}})^{2}\sqrt{{y}_{\text{new}}})\cdot 1 \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2}\sqrt{y}+\frac{1}{2}({x}_{\text{new}})^{2}\sqrt{{y}_{\text{new}}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting this into ${y}_{\text{new}}=y+Δy,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{\text{new}} & =y+Δy \\ {y}_{\text{new}} & =y+\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2}\sqrt{y}+\frac{1}{2}({x}_{\text{new}})^{2}\sqrt{{y}_{\text{new}}},\end{aligned}
$$

and moving all terms to the left-hand side gives the equation

$$
{y}_{\text{new}}-\frac{1}{2}({x}_{\text{new}})^{2}\sqrt{{y}_{\text{new}}}-y-\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2}\sqrt{y}=0.
$$

So, the general form of the function $g$ for step size $Δx=1$ is

$$
g({y}_{\text{new}})={y}_{\text{new}}-\frac{1}{2}({x}_{\text{new}})^{2}\sqrt{{y}_{\text{new}}}-y-\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2}\sqrt{y}.
$$

Now, in the first step, the new $x$ value is

$$
{x}_{\text{new}}=x+Δx=1+1=2.
$$

Therefore, the function used in the first step is

$$
\begin{aligned}g({y}_{\text{new}}) & ={y}_{\text{new}}-\frac{1}{2}(2)^{2}\sqrt{{y}_{\text{new}}}-1-\frac{1}{2}(1)^{2}\sqrt{1} \\  & ={y}_{\text{new}}-2\sqrt{{y}_{\text{new}}}-\frac{3}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186229157 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186228908 :question/id #uuid "d77c4a1b-863b-57ad-be77-44f2d802f554" :question/math-academy-id "e-21677"} :knowledge-point/id $$
{y}^{′}=3x-{y}^{3},\,y(0)=1
$$

Use the trapezoidal method with one step and Newton's method to approximate $y(1).$ Round your answer to two decimal places.

$$
{y}^{′}=f(x,y),\,y(a)=c,
$$

the trapezoidal method with step size $Δx$ is given by

$$
Δy=\frac{1}{2}({y}^{′}+{y}_{\text{new}}^{′})\cdot Δx,
$$

with ${y}_{\text{new}}^{′}=f({x}_{\text{new}},{y}_{\text{new}})$ evaluated at the next $x$ and $y$ values.

Since we want to find the value of $y$ at $x=1,$ we will use a step size of

$$
Δx=1-0=1.
$$

Now, let's proceed with the trapezoidal method. In general, $Δy$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}Δy & =\frac{1}{2}({y}^{′}+{y}_{\text{new}}^{′})\cdot Δx \\  & =\frac{1}{2}((3x-{y}^{3})+(3{x}_{\text{new}}-({y}_{\text{new}})^{3}))\cdot 1 \\  & =1.5x-0.5{y}^{3}+1.5{x}_{\text{new}}-0.5({y}_{\text{new}})^{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting this into ${y}_{\text{new}}=y+Δy,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{\text{new}} & =y+Δy \\ {y}_{\text{new}} & =y+1.5x-0.5{y}^{3}+1.5{x}_{\text{new}}-0.5({y}_{\text{new}})^{3},\end{aligned}
$$

and moving all terms to the left-hand side gives the equation

$$
0.5({y}_{\text{new}})^{3}+{y}_{\text{new}}+0.5{y}^{3}-y-1.5{x}_{\text{new}}-1.5x=0.
$$

So, the general form of the function $g$ for step size $Δx=1$ is

$$
g({y}_{\text{new}})=0.5({y}_{\text{new}})^{3}+{y}_{\text{new}}+0.5{y}^{3}-y-1.5{x}_{\text{new}}-1.5x.
$$

Now, in the first step, the new $x$ value is

$$
{x}_{\text{new}}=x+Δx=0+1=1.
$$

 Then, the function $g$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}g({y}_{\text{new}}) & =0.5({y}_{\text{new}})^{3}+{y}_{\text{new}}+0.5(1)^{3}-1-1.5\cdot 1-1.5\cdot 0 \\  & =0.5({y}_{\text{new}})^{3}+{y}_{\text{new}}+0.5-1-1.5 \\  & =0.5({y}_{\text{new}})^{3}+{y}_{\text{new}}-2.\end{aligned}
$$

We use a root-finding method with starting point $y=1$ to solve $g({y}_{\text{new}})=0.$ We'll use Newton's method:

$$
({y}_{\text{new}})_{n+1}=({y}_{\text{new}})_{n}-\frac{g({y}_{\text{new}})}{{g}^{′}({y}_{\text{new}})}.
$$

Note that the derivative of $g$ is

$$
{g}^{′}({y}_{\text{new}})=1.5({y}_{\text{new}})^{2}+1.
$$

Therefore, our Newton's method iterative scheme is as follows:

$$
({y}_{\text{new}})_{n+1}=({y}_{\text{new}})_{n}-\frac{0.5(({y}_{\text{new}})_{n})^{3}+({y}_{\text{new}})_{n}-2}{1.5(({y}_{\text{new}})_{n})^{2}+1}.
$$

Applying several iterations of Newton's method starting with $y(0)=1,$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}({y}_{\text{new}})_{1} & =1 \\ ({y}_{\text{new}})_{2} & =1.2 \\ ({y}_{\text{new}})_{3} & ≈1.179\,747 \\ ({y}_{\text{new}})_{4} & ≈1.179\,509\end{aligned}
$$

:tutorial/content "We know how to apply the trapezoidal method to initial value problems that are linear in $y.$ Can we apply it to more complex initial value problems, such as

$$
y' = 2x^2 - y^4, \qquad y(0)=1?
$$

Yes, we can. To do so, we define a function $g$ such that the next $y$-value, $y_\text{new},$ satisfies the equation $g(y_\text{new})=0.$ Then, we apply a root-finding method to solve for $y_\text{new}.$

To demonstrate, let's apply the trapezoidal method to the IVP above with step size $\Delta x = 0.5.$

We begin as usual. In general, the change $\Delta y$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}Δy & =\frac{1}{2}({y}^{'}+{y}_{\text{new}}^{'})\cdot Δx \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(2{x}^{2}-{y}^{4}+2({x}_{\text{new}})^{2}-({y}_{\text{new}})^{4})\cdot 0.5 \\  & =0.5{x}^{2}-0.25{y}^{4}+0.5({x}_{\text{new}})^{2}-0.25({y}_{\text{new}})^{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting this into the update formula for $\Delta y,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{\text{new}} & =y+Δy \\ {y}_{\text{new}} & =y+0.5{x}^{2}-0.25{y}^{4}+0.5({x}_{\text{new}})^{2}-0.25({y}_{\text{new}})^{4},\end{aligned}
$$

and moving all terms to the left-hand side gives the equation

$$
0.25(y_\text{new})^4 + y_\text{new} + 0.25y^4 - y - 0.5x^2 - 0.5(x_\text{new})^2 = 0.
$$

Here, there is no simple algebraic rearrangement to isolate $y_\text{new},$ so solving exactly is impractical.
Instead, we define a new function $g$ of $y_\text{new}$ by the expression on the left-hand side:

$$
g(y_\text{new}) = 0.25(y_\text{new})^4 + y_\text{new} + 0.25y^4 - y - 0.5x^2 - 0.5(x_\text{new})^2
$$

Note that $x,$ $y,$ and $x_\text{new}$ are known constants at each step, so $g$ is truly a one-variable function in $y_\text{new}.$

Then, the next $y$-value $y_\text{new}$ is a root of this function: $g(y_\text{new}) = 0.$ Therefore, to find $y_\text{new},$ we apply a root-finding method, such as Newton's method.

For instance, in the first step, the new $x$-value is $x_\text{new} = 0 + 0.5 = 0.5.$ So, the function used in the first step is

$$
\begin{aligned}g({y}_{\text{new}}) & =0.25({y}_{\text{new}})^{4}+{y}_{\text{new}}+0.25\cdot (1)^{4}-1-0.5\cdot (0)^{2}-0.5\cdot (0.5)^{2} \\  & =0.25({y}_{\text{new}})^{4}+{y}_{\text{new}}-0.875.\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we would proceed to use a root-finding method with starting point $y=1$ to solve $g(y_\text{new})=0.$" :tutorial/id #uuid "9cd9bd37-323b-5d8a-8d1f-4d8924a59da0" :tutorial/math-academy-id 14495 problems that are linear in $y.$ Can we apply it to more complex initial value problems, such as

$$
y' = 2x^2 - y^4, \qquad y(0)=1?
$$

Yes, we can. To do so, we define a function $g$ such that the next $y$-value, $y_\text{new},$ satisfies the equation $g(y_\text{new})=0.$ Then, we apply a root-finding method to solve for $y_\text{new}.$

To demonstrate, let's apply the trapezoidal method to the IVP above with step size $\Delta x = 0.5.$

We begin as usual. In general, the change $\Delta y$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}Δy & =\frac{1}{2}({y}^{'}+{y}_{\text{new}}^{'})\cdot Δx \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(2{x}^{2}-{y}^{4}+2({x}_{\text{new}})^{2}-({y}_{\text{new}})^{4})\cdot 0.5 \\  & =0.5{x}^{2}-0.25{y}^{4}+0.5({x}_{\text{new}})^{2}-0.25({y}_{\text{new}})^{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting this into the update formula for $\Delta y,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{\text{new}} & =y+Δy \\ {y}_{\text{new}} & =y+0.5{x}^{2}-0.25{y}^{4}+0.5({x}_{\text{new}})^{2}-0.25({y}_{\text{new}})^{4},\end{aligned}
$$

and moving all terms to the left-hand side gives the equation

$$
0.25(y_\text{new})^4 + y_\text{new} + 0.25y^4 - y - 0.5x^2 - 0.5(x_\text{new})^2 = 0.
$$

Here, there is no simple algebraic rearrangement to isolate $y_\text{new},$ so solving exactly is impractical.
Instead, we define a new function $g$ of $y_\text{new}$ by the expression on the left-hand side:

$$
g(y_\text{new}) = 0.25(y_\text{new})^4 + y_\text{new} + 0.25y^4 - y - 0.5x^2 - 0.5(x_\text{new})^2
$$

Note that $x,$ $y,$ and $x_\text{new}$ are known constants at each step, so $g$ is truly a one-variable function in $y_\text{new}.$

Then, the next $y$-value $y_\text{new}$ is a root of this function: $g(y_\text{new}) = 0.$ Therefore, to find $y_\text{new},$ we apply a root-finding method, such as Newton's method.

For instance, in the first step, the new $x$-value is $x_\text{new} = 0 + 0.5 = 0.5.$ So, the function used in the first step is

$$
\begin{aligned}g({y}_{\text{new}}) & =0.25({y}_{\text{new}})^{4}+{y}_{\text{new}}+0.25\cdot (1)^{4}-1-0.5\cdot (0)^{2}-0.5\cdot (0.5)^{2} \\  & =0.25({y}_{\text{new}})^{4}+{y}_{\text{new}}-0.875.\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we would proceed to use a root-finding method with starting point $y=1$ to solve $g(y_\text{new})=0.$" :tutorial/id #uuid "9cd9bd37-323b-5d8a-8d1f-4d8924a59da0" :tutorial/math-academy-id 14495 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "3c9d3bf2-ca7c-52cb-b895-adf1cf0cbed3" :step/math-academy-id 594484 :step/next {:db/id 17592186230033}} {:db/id 17592186230186 :tutorial/content "We know how to apply the trapezoidal method to initial value problems that are linear in $y.$ Can we apply it to more complex initial value problems, such as

that are linear in $y.$ Can we apply it to more complex initial value problems, such as

$$
y' = 2x^2 - y^4, \qquad y(0)=1?
$$

Yes, we can. To do so, we define a function $g$ such that the next $y$-value, $y_\text{new},$ satisfies the equation $g(y_\text{new})=0.$ Then, we apply a root-finding method to solve for $y_\text{new}.$

To demonstrate, let's apply the trapezoidal method to the IVP above with step size $\Delta x = 0.5.$

We begin as usual. In general, the change $\Delta y$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}Δy & =\frac{1}{2}({y}^{'}+{y}_{\text{new}}^{'})\cdot Δx \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(2{x}^{2}-{y}^{4}+2({x}_{\text{new}})^{2}-({y}_{\text{new}})^{4})\cdot 0.5 \\  & =0.5{x}^{2}-0.25{y}^{4}+0.5({x}_{\text{new}})^{2}-0.25({y}_{\text{new}})^{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting this into the update formula for $\Delta y,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{\text{new}} & =y+Δy \\ {y}_{\text{new}} & =y+0.5{x}^{2}-0.25{y}^{4}+0.5({x}_{\text{new}})^{2}-0.25({y}_{\text{new}})^{4},\end{aligned}
$$

and moving all terms to the left-hand side gives the equation

$$
0.25(y_\text{new})^4 + y_\text{new} + 0.25y^4 - y - 0.5x^2 - 0.5(x_\text{new})^2 = 0.
$$

Here, there is no simple algebraic rearrangement to isolate $y_\text{new},$ so solving exactly is impractical.
Instead, we define a new function $g$ of $y_\text{new}$ by the expression on the left-hand side:

$$
